content.thinking:
I need to pin down the facts for the postmortem: the symptom is that shoppers' stored monthly spend totals don't reconcile with actual purchases, with the alert showing all 240 totals affected, and monthly statements rendering the wrong total using total_this_month_cents, though there's no evidence users actually noticed.

Tracing the causal chain, each purchase made while the monthly-spend feature flag was on updated total_cents but skipped updating total_this_month_cents, so the shortfall equals the price of every purchase recorded under that path. That path only ran because the flag was flipped on at a specific point, selecting the derive_the_month=True branch — and I'm checking the deploy history and change records to confirm there were no other deploys or changes in that window that could have contributed, since the flag flip appears to be the only relevant change.

The replica restarts happened after the onset, so they're ruled out as a trigger. Now I'm figuring out how to order the five-whys chain: symptom, then why the total was wrong, then why that derive path was taken, then why the flag was allowed to cause harm (no reconciliation check existed for that path), landing on the missing update as the root cause.

The root cause is that with the monthly-spend feature on, purchases got routed through a path that updates purchase history and total spend but never updates the month-specific total, leaving each month's recorded total short by every purchase price after the flag flipped. I'm phrasing the plain-language version as "likely" since it's inferred, and confirming this conclusion rests only on the one row showing the behavior, not on direct reads of the derive function itself.

Since the flag was left on and never reverted, new purchases will keep leaving month totals short, and the already-wrong stored totals still feed into monthly statements, usual-spend comparisons, and averages—so I should state this risk in one sentence without implying Argus handed off anything beyond leaving the toggle for a person to fix.

Now I'm looking at contributing factors: first, there was no test verifying the monthly-derivation path stays in sync with purchases before the flag flipped on, which the fix's added tests should address. Second, the spend-integrity check only runs every several days, letting the fault go undetected for a while—this gap isn't addressed by the existing fix, so I should propose a more frequent reconciliation check as a detection improvement.

I'm also noting that the alert didn't page anyone or link to an incident, so nobody acted on it—routing that alert to page on-call seems like a reasonable fix. The rollout scope for the flag change is unclear, so I'll skip that one, but I should record that error rate wasn't actually measured, since metrics appearing flat was just an assumption rather than verified data.

For action items, repairing the wrongly written totals should be a human-driven step: run the repair script as a dry run against exported accounts first, review its report, then apply the fix and write back the corrected totals. I should also flag any accounts the repair script finds with a month total exceeding their actual purchases for investigation.

For detection, I want more frequent spend-integrity checks, reconciliation runs triggered right after any flag change touching the purchase ledger, and on-call paging for SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile. For prevention, I should require tests confirming both flag states produce matching accounts before any flag selecting a ledger path goes live in production.

Checking the division-by-zero risk in the bought-length calculations, it doesn't seem related here, so I'll skip that. I'm also considering whether to flag the monthly statements and spend summaries generated from affected accounts since the issue began, to determine if corrected versions need to go out to shoppers.

For lessons learned, I note that Argus correctly placed the onset timing and linked it to the flag change, reading the flag history to establish that connection.

Code-Fix proposed a draft fix with tests and a repair script in PR #348 after the alert was raised, which was a solid response. Argus also did well by declining to take an action it couldn't verify, opting to recommend instead. On the downside, the investigator failed to review the logs.

I'm reconsidering whether that's really a gap or just a limitation of what the record shows, since nobody actually read those logs. The metrics window only covered a short span before the alert, nowhere near its actual onset, which is another limitation rather than a clear failure. I'm leaning toward leaving went_wrong empty since the real issues seem to be limits of the record rather than concrete mistakes, and for got_lucky, it looks like there was no customer loss.

For assumptions, I'm noting that the onset is taken as the oldest affected purchase, bounded by the integrity check data; that the mechanism relies on Code-Fix's interpretation; that the impact figures are lower bounds; and that the flag stayed on at the end, with reactivation left to a person rather than an automated process. I also note no deployment came back and the revision remains unnamed, and it's unclear whether shoppers actually saw wrong totals on their statements. I'm being careful not to include specific figures in the prose.

I need to avoid stray numbers or quantity words while still conveying the timing — using phrases tied to the citation labels instead of literal figures, and referring to the draft pull request rather than its number to stay safe. The citation chain starts with the first assumption label, then moves into the fault and reconciliation evidence showing how the monthly total comparison works against purchases.

Now I'm working out step three: the flag turns on at the cited point, backed by the policy and trace labels, with the fault note confirming that's the path it selects. Deploys and replica starts get ruled out by timing evidence, and since no earlier change was read in the window, I note that explicitly rather than implying something was checked and excluded.

action_items.item: Export the shopper accounts, run the repair script from the draft pull request as a dry run against them, and review the report it writes.
After the dry-run report has been reviewed, run the repair script with --apply and write the corrected month totals back to the store.
Look into any accounts the repair script reports as having a month total above their purchases, which the script leaves unchanged.
Find the monthly statements and spend summaries produced from affected accounts since {began}, and decide whether shoppers need corrected ones.
Require a test showing that every flag-selected purchase-ledger path returns the same account as the default path before such a flag can be switched on in production.
Run the spend-integrity reconciliation much more often than every {A5} days.
Run the spend reconciliation automatically shortly after any flag change that touches how purchases are recorded.
Route SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile so that it pages the on-call engineer.

causal_chain.step: Shopper spend totals stopped matching the purchases behind them: {A1} of {A2} checked totals did not reconcile, the widest was short by {A3}, and the oldest affected purchase was recorded at {A4}.

The stored month total, `total_this_month_cents`, fell behind the sum of the month's purchases. The reconciliation compares that field with the sum of this month's purchase prices, so a stale field shows up as a shortfall. Code-Fix's reading of the source says `record_purchase_deriving_the_month` adds each purchase to the history and moves `total_cents` but never moves `total_this_month_cents`, which would leave each purchase recorded that way missing from the month total.

ruled_out.what: A deploy: the production change events read back only the flag change, and no deploys came back over the window searched.
The current replicas starting: all of them started at {T7.3}, after the onset, so their start cannot have begun it.

causal_chain.step: Purchases were being recorded on that path because the monthly-spend-feature flag was switched on at {P1.1}, which is the only change the flag provider's history shows in the hour before the onset. Code-Fix's reading says this flag selects the `derive_the_month=True` path. The first affected purchase came {began - P1.1} after the switch. The change history read held no other change, so no earlier change could be weighed.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching on a new monthly-spend feature likely sent every purchase down a route that records the purchase but never adds its price to the shopper's running total for the month, so those stored totals fell behind what shoppers had actually bought.

contributing_factors.factor: No test or check was seen confirming that the path the flag selects keeps the stored month total in step with the purchases, or that it returns the same account as the default path, before the flag was switched on in production.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The missing month-total update would have been caught before the flag went on, and no shopper total would have been written short.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The fault was found only by the spend-integrity check, which runs every {A5} days, and no check was seen reconciling totals after the flag change.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The shortfall would have been flagged soon after the switch rather than {alerted_after_the_onset} after the onset, so far fewer totals would have been written wrong.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: The SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been told at once and could have put the flag back, an action Argus left for a person, rather than it waiting on someone noticing the recommendation.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well: Argus read the flag provider's history and found the monthly-spend-feature switch {T13.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
Argus did not take an action it could not verify inside the time it waits. It recommended putting the flag back instead.
Code-Fix proposed a fix, tests and a repair script as a draft pull request {T18.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, `record_a_purchase` takes the `derive_the_month=True` path. That path calls `record_purchase_deriving_the_month`, which adds the purchase to the history and moves `total_cents` but never moves `total_this_month_cents`. So every purchase recorded on that path left the stored month total short by that purchase's price. Nothing raised an error, because the field was stale rather than missing.
input.still_at_risk: With monthly-spend-feature still on, purchases recorded on that path could keep leaving month totals short, and the totals that are already wrong are still read by shoppers' monthly statements, the comparison with their usual spending and the per-item spend averages.
input.symptom: Shoppers' stored monthly spend totals fell short of the purchases behind them
